speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The Quartermaster
General, General Asihton; at Lindsay, Lt.-Col. White.

We happen to have in the committee this afternoon distinguished soldiers who have made a name for themselves in the British Empire and the world over. Perhaps it is not always that we have the benefit of their counsel and assistance in a committee of this kind when we are dealing with military matters. There was never anything happened in Canada that gave such a shock to the community and the ordnary layman as the reputation that the Ross rifle obtained. I am a mere layman, knowing nothing about military matters, but I could not help hearing these things. The military men who are in this chamber know what has been the report- that many of our young men have been killed by reason of the baulking and refusal to act of the Ross rifles. Men used to get their hands burned and smashed, and this rifle would not work at all. That has been the report, and there is in this country many a sad heart where a son or more than one had been killed and the father or mother believes that he or they could not have been killed if a better rifle than the Ross rifle had been furnished. That report is abroad in the land. If it is not true, it should be forever set at rest and the public of this country satisfied that such things did not occur. If the report is true that such things occurred, the Ross rifle should not be mentioned in this country again in connection with military matters; it should be scrapped and never put into the hands of anybody if it is such a weapon as we were made to believe that it was. Perhaps we shall never have a better opportunity of settling this matter once and for all than while we are in this committee and have present with us distinguished soldiers who have had experience in con-

nection with this rifle. When they pass from the scene, we shall have nobody with the same first-hand knowledge of this matter that they have. Perhaps this is not the time or the place to discuss that matter; if not, I shall not expect it, but I do think that the Militia Department should set at rest once and for all this controversy about the Ross rifle.

I would like to hear a word from a soldier, a practical man of war, who has used the Ross rifle. I have never used that rifle myself but a very particular friend of mine, a medical man, who has a great reputation as a hunter, and who has used practically every kind of sporting and military rifle there is, about two years ago was very nearly killed by a Ross rifle that he was shooting with. Something went wrong with the mechanism, and the check flew back and struck him on the bridge of the nose, almost blinding him. He had a very narrow escape with his life. I would like to know if the Ross rifle is worth bothering with any more as a rifle for practical purposes in the field of war. My information from returned soldiers is that it is not a suitable weapon in the trenches.

The story of the Ross rifle, in brief, is that it was introduced into the Canadian militia some time in 1902 or 1903. Up to that time, the Canadian militia had been armed with the long Lee-Enfield, which had been used successfully in the South African war. I have never been able to understand why it was considered necessary that we here in Canada should have a rifle pattern of our own. It is of the very essence of co-operation in military service that all the material which is used shall be standard. Therefore, I think it was a mistake in the first instance to introduce our own rifle which differed from the rifle in use throughout the rest of the Empire. The argument advanced at that time was that it was desirable in the manufacture of rifles that we should be independent, and have a factory of our own and make our own rifles. That argument would be perfectly good still, if we made a standard rifle, but it was decided that we should have a rifle pattern of our own, the latest thing in rifles, and so the Ross rifle came into being. A factory was established at Quebec and the arming of the Canadian militia with the Ross rifle began in 1902 or thereabouts.
My first experience with the rifle was in 1908, when I was attending a board test

of fifty of these rifles in rapid fire. Four per cent of these rifles jammed in the test. Something went wrong with the chamber; there was some weakness in the extractor; after the explosion, the cartridge stuck in the breech and the extractor would not extract it. That seems to have been the difficulty throughout. That was reported on in that year; I was the chairman of the board at that time. After that, the Ross rifle became a political football for the political parties. A lot of men defended it who did not know anything about a rifle, and a lot of men attacked it, who knew less. When the war broke out, the Canadian militia was armed with the Ross rifle, and there at once came a demand all over the world for rifles. It must be assumed that any rifle is better than none at all, and so the Canadian force proceeded overseas armed with the Ross rifle. The unfortunate part of it was-I will say that in favour of the rifle at the moment-that the country was fairly well divided on the value of the Ross rifle. There had been propaganda against it, but on the other hand there were those who favoured it. As a single-shot rifle, as distinct from rapid fire, the Ross rifle was satisfactory; that is to say, in firing single shot there was no heating of the barrel, and generally the extractor worked and the empty shell was withdrawn. There were rapid fire Lists of the Ross rifle in Canada prior to t ie war, at various places and times, and in all these tests a certain number of the rifles would jam That fact was known.
The first severe fighting in which the Canadian troops became engaged was at the battle of Ypres, in April, 1915.' While I was not there, I have been told by hundreds of people-it is a matter of common knowledge, there is no question about it-that the Ross rifles jammed in rapid fire. Those who defend the rifles say, first, that the men were not trained in the manipulation of the bolt. Well, a military rifle should not be so intricate that a man of ordinary intelligence cannot learn to operate the bolt. Next, it was said in favour of the rifle that the ammunition was bad, or at all events was unsuitable to the rifle. Well, troops should not be armed with a rifle that is not suited to all the ammunition supplied. There were six or seven brands of ammunition in use at that time, and the British rifle used them all. I do not know anybody who ever had a Lee-Enfield rifle jam with any of the ammunition that was supplied, though I have heard that they sometimes

did. The fact 3s undoubted that the Ross rifle did jam at the battle of Ypres. Now, if you arm a hundred men with Ross rifles, and it is said before the battle begins that the rifle may jam, the morale of your troops is lowered at the very start. For instance, if you went out to hunt a grizzly bear that was known to be very vicious, you would not stand up when it charged if you had a rifle that you thought might go wrong. Well, there was a tremendous amount of jamming of the Ross rifles. Scarcely any of them stood up under lengthy fire, and the morale of the Canadian troops was seriously damaged in consequence. At the conclusion of the battle, our men threw their rifles away and picked up British rifles that were lying all over the battlefield. It is a matter of common knowledge Ross rifles were lying in heaps all over the place. That is the story of the first division.
I do not understand how the men could secure the Lee-Enfield rifle on the battlefield.
There were thousands of British dead lying around.
What about the first part of the battle?

In the early part of the battle the Canadian troops were using the Ross rifle, but as they moved about the field they would pick up a Lee-Enfield and throw their Ross rifle away. As I have said, the Ross rifles were lying in heaps all over the field at the end of the battle. Finally they were armed with the Lee-Enfield rifle and never had anything more to do with the Ross.
Then the Second Division came over to France armed with the Ross rifle. In the meantime, there had been a great deal of tinkering with the Ross rifle in England, reaming out the breach and strengthening the bolt head, and then there were divided opinions as to whether what was being done to the bolt head was doing it more harm than good. Immediately there was a difference of opinion on that question, and there was a sort of political line-up, one might say, on the issue. The Second Division was pretty closely watched, and I may say that an order was issued in that division threatening rigorous punishment to any man who possessed himself of a Lee-Enfield rifle. I have a copy of that order. Then the Third Division came out armed with the Ross rifle, with the exception of the Princess Patricia's, who had never
been armed with that rifle. There was considerable discussion regarding the merits of the Ross rifle, and the Third Division troops, who had somewhat more to do with the First Division troops than had the Second Division, coming more in contact with the men of the First Division, were told all about the Ross rifle; and the men of the First Division, by their conversation, very seriously impaired the confidence of the Third Division in the Ross rifle. Indeed, so much so was this that we felt called upon to see whether we could not re-establish confidence in that rifle. At that time we were informed that we should have to use the Ross rifle because there were no Lee-Enfield's to be had. I desire to lay stress on that point.
At what period of the war was that?

I am speaking now
of the period from November, 1915, onward. The Second Division arrived in France with the Ross rifles in September, 1915. The Third Division was formed early in January, or thereabouts, of 1916, although some of the troops of that division had been in France prior to that time, and they were the men who were talked to by men of the First Division. We were told-I do not know that I can cite authority-that we should have to use the Ross rifle because there were no Lee-Enfield rifles available for issue. As to the truth of that, I can express no opinion, but I do know that, whether or not there were other rifles to be had, we were told that the Ross rifle was the only one available. In order to try to restore confidence on the part of the men in the Ross rifle I conducted a test in my own unit. I had one hundred men of each company fire, or attempt to fire, one hundred rounds at a target, rapid fire, and I turned in the results of the test. Some of the rifles jammed at as low as the third round, while the highest number of rounds fired in rapid fire was sixty. There was one man who got off, I think, about ninety rounds. Now, the rifles were clean, the ammunition was selected, and the men were specially trained, because the test was put on with a view to demonstrating that the rifle was all right. But the test had the contrary effect. It demonstrated that the rifle was not all right, and so far as morale was concerned, the condition was worse then than before, because what theretofore had been merely doubt, became more or less certainty. Then came service in the trenches.

Did the hundred men
in question make a test with any other rifle under rapid fire?

No. There were
four hundred men, one hundred from each of four companies, each man firing one hundred rounds of ammunition. There was no necessity for a test of the Lee-Enfield because its reliability was not in question by the troops who had used both or either. On the first of May we were attacked quite heavily and rapid fire was opened. The two companies with which I was connected slackened fire, and I went amongst them. I discovered that the rifles were jammed, and the actual statistics showed that one company averaged, I think, twenty-seven rounds. In another company their record was not strictly accurate, but they informed me that two-thirds of the rifles had jammed. I found the men trying to open the bolts of the rifles with their boots, and some tried to beat the bolts open with their entrenching tools. I found the men in a very bad way, using expressive language, while some of them were almost crying. Altogether the situation was pretty bad. I promised them that they would never have to use the Ross rifle again, although I had no authority to make such a promise. I told them, however, to help themselves to Lee-Enfield rifles whenever they could, and thereupon there sprang up a traffic between my men and the men in the British hospitals. The price of the Lee-Enfield was five francs. A man going to a British hospital would put his rifle in charge of the orderly, and get a check for it, and the orderly was willing to put a Ross rifle in its place for five francs. In that way I almost succeeded in re-arming my battalion with Lee-Enfields. Then came some fighting at Hooge, and the Ross rifles again jammed.
Did the private himself have to pay the five francs in order to get the Lee Enfield?

The private himself paid it. We were armed partly with Ross rifles and partly with Lee Enfields. In the meantime, attempts had been made to get an issue of Lee Enfield rifles authorized. We were first of all confronted with the statement that it was difficult to get Lee-Enfields because there were not enough of them, and of course one was also conscious of the fact that the old discussion still persisted and that there were still friends of the Ross. However, after the fighting at Ypres in June an order was
[Mr. Griesbach. 1
finally issued re-anming everybody with the Lee Enfield.
The member for Mackenzie (Mr. Reid), speaks of the danger of the bolt blowing out. As a matter of fact, if the Ross rifle has anything to recommend it, apart from its accuracy-because it is a very accurate rifle-it is the fact that, in the interlocking of the bolthead, it is a stronger rifile than almost any other, because the bolt-head interlocks at the base, and the chamber has really a stronger bolt-blocking than almost any other rifle I know of. I do not recall having heard of any Ross rifle bolts blowing out, but I have heard of this having happened in connection with Lee-Enfields. Of course, there may possibly have been bolts that blew out on Ross rifles, but that is not the objection to that rifle. It would be a technical defect in any event, and would not amount to very much. The fatal objection is that it will not stand up to rapid fire because it jams, and that has been proved absolutely to the hilt. There cannot be much discussion on that point. But in addition to this fatal defect, there was the question of the desirability of our having the same riffle as used by the troops from other parts of the Empire. We were going to cooperate with them, and there was no reason why we should not have the same equipment, because they have the facilities and the means for the testing of military equipment in England, and they are willing to spend more time and money in this direction than we can.
The hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) raises another question. A good deal has been said on the subject the hon. member has brought up, that as a result of being armed with the Ross rifle many men were killed. I really do not know how just that accusation is.
I heard it made by a man who lost his son at Ypres in 1916. It was very unjust for two or three reasons. First, the son was serving in the Princess Patricias who were armed with the Lee-Enfield, not the Ross rifle at all. In the second place it was purely an artillery encounter and our men might just as well have been armed with shotguns in that particular battle. In the first battle of Ypres there was no doubt the firing of the Canadian troops was very much less effective, and the enemy enjoyed a certain immunity, from the fact that the Canadians were armed with an inferior weapon. It might be possible that in that engagement there were advantages to the enemy and disadvantages to us which re-

suited in heavier casualties, but at that time I do not think there was very much doubt that no other rifle was to be had, no other rifle was available.
Now that is the story of the Ross rifle as I know it. I never had any use for it myself. I discouraged the use of the weapon at its inception-I thought its use unwise and unsound. I knew that it was defective in its bolt manipulation and rapid fire and absolutely proved it to be so by actual use. As I have said, it is a very accurate rifle, there are very few more accurate rifles than the Ross. But it is not a military weapon which stands up to the tests which actual warfare put upon it.

May I ask the minister
if they are making Ross rifles in Canada, and if so whether it comes under this vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No, the manufacture
was discontinued three years ago.

Are you still using
them in the service at all?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No, we are not using
them.

Would it not be a
wise policy to provide the young soldier, from the very inception of his training up to the time he would have to go into actual warfare, with the very best arm available? Is it not a mistake to allow our young men to be trained in the use of a rifle that is defective. I am very much obliged to the distinguished general (Mr. Griesbach) for the history of the Ross rifle which he gave a few moments ago, but it is not at all clear that grievous mistakes have not been made in connection with the use of this rifle. It is a sad thing that we ever had occasion to use it. I am afraid it has aroused the painful impression that it may have been instrumental in causing the death of many of our young men. I would suggest having nothing further do to with this rifle. If there is any material in it that can be put to any good purpose I suppose that should be done; but the Government would be well advised to get rid of it altogether. The Ross rifle should be used no more by our militia.

I am not unmindful of
the fact that the minister welcomes recognition of reduction in expenditure in his department. I notice that this item has been reduced this year by the sum of $25,000 and I would ask the reason for that?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It is for the remodelling of the arms in our ordnance stores, it is thought we can get along with a smaller amount than we did last year. The work will be curtailed this year, and I trust will be a litle further curtailed next year.

Is there a rifle being
made under the auspices of the Government of Canada? If so, where is it being made, what is the pattern, and what is the number?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Not at present; we are not manufacturing any rifle.

Do I understand there
is an inspector of textiles in connection with the department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
There is, and he has
the inspection of all our clothing and the like. His name is included in the Civil Government Estimates.

What salary does he
draw?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: A salary of $2,800.
Is there an assistant in his office?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There was, but not this year.
What use is now being made of the arsenal at Quebec?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: They are manufacturing both ,small-arm ammunition and some 18-pounder ammunition, I think about four and a half million rounds of the former.
What is the rifle?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The service rifle, the Lee-Enfield that we are using.
Where are you getting the Lee-Enfields?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: At the end of the war a large number of them returned with the troops from England.
They are not being made in Canada?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No.'

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Pay of Staff, $265,000.
What staffs are included in this item?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The headquarters and district staffs.
Is the Militia Council included?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
Is the salary of the vicepresident of the Militia Council included in this also?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
And that of the general staff and of the different branches in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
May I ask the minister to give us the number of officers whose salaries are covered by this item, and also the number of non-commissioned officers and men?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This applies to fifty officers including the officers in the headquarters and the staffs of all the military districts in Canada-for the headquarters, $98,400; for the districts, $154,700. There is a general balance left for contingencies of $11,000.
How much of this amount is voted for the non-commissioned officers and men and how much for the officers?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is no pay for the non-commissioned officers in this item.
It is only for the officers?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Just-for the headquarters and district staffs.
There is no other expenditure under this item than the salaries of staff officers?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is right.
How many of those officers are above the rank of colonel?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The vice-president of the Militia Council is a major-general.
Who is he?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Major-General Fiset.
The chief of the general staff is a major-general; the quartermaster-general is also a major-general.
Who are they?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The quartermastergeneral is Major Ashton. The chief of the general staff is General MacBrien. The adjutant general is General Elmsley; the master-general of ordnance is General Morrison.
In the headquarters of the military districts how many officers have we above the rank of lieutenant-colonel?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: In No. 1 district there is only one over the rank of lieutenant-colonel, General Panet; in No. 2 district, General Williams; in No. 3 district, General King. General Hill has the overseas rank of brigadier-general. In No. 4 district, General Armstrong is the only one above the rank of lieutenant-colonel.
What district is No. 4?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Montreal. In No. 5, Quebec, General Landry; No. 6, St. John, General McDonald; No. 7, Halifax, General Thacker; Nos. 8 and 9 districts do not exist.
Where are they?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not think they ever had any existence at all.
There are thirteen districts?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No. 10 is Winnipeg, General Ketchen; No. 11, Victoria, General Ross; No. 12, Regina, General Orme; No. 13, General Bell.
The minister has evidently forgotten some of them. He has a general here, for instance, General Bur-stall. .

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: He is not in the districts; he is inspector-general with headquarters at Ottawa.
Would the minister give the names of other generals in Ottawa who are not connected with the Militia Council?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Inspector-General Bur-stall is the only one.
I hate to correct the minister, but I know of another general, a very gallant soldier, Brigadier-General Swift.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: He retired four or five months ago.

He was in the service
up to about two months ago.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: He retired in January.

Has the principle ever been considered of enlarging the districts and in that way decreasing the staffs?
I may be wrong, but it occurs to me, if war is practically relegated to the far distant future, as we all hope, that as a matter of economy the minister might take into consideration the idea that springs from my inquiry-a reduction in the personnel, even if all those who are now in the service should be pensioned liberally, realizing

as I do that men who have engaged in a military occupation have a claim on the country's service as they have unfitted themselves for any other occupation. I believe it would popularize the Government if in the quest of economy they would proceed along the lines of reducing military expenditure, and I offer this suggestion as one way of achieving that result, if not on these Estimates at least at some future time.
I believe public opinion would be strongly behind the Government if they would make some effort to remodel the service by enlarging the districts and reducing the staffs. I am speaking without knowledge of the subject, but I would like to have an expression of view, in the hope that something may come of it in the country's best interests.

I think the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) struck the right note when he said that he was talking without knowledge of the subject. Any one conversant with the principles of military organization knows that the system of districts in one form or another is used in all armies. The two districts, Nos. 8 and 9, were never set up. I for one would be strongly opposed to cutting down the staffs of the districts; if anything, I think they are too small. Coming back to the war, there is a certain public opinion in this country and you cannot mention anything about the militia unless some fool shouts "Militarism!" You cannot throw militarism around a man like a blanket, militarism is a state of mind. It takes a century or more to make a people militaristic, and you could not make the Canadian people militaristic in a century. The only opposite means of maintaining the defence of a country, if you do not want conscription, is to maintain a strong voluntary organization, and in order to do that you have to have military districts. A lot of brilliant young soldiers came back from the war who desired to keep up soldiering-I did not, I had all the soldiering I wanted-and they were trying to establish a system under which we would have permanent adjutants, sergeants, and orderly-room clerks. But the country would not stand for this extra expense, so we have lost all those bright young men, and I think we made a great mistake, for they would have been a great source of strength to our militia organization. I should be very much opposed to the cutting down of the military districts. I think it would be a great mistake. If we are going to have any kind
of organization we must have the division of districts. I am as strong against militarism and conscription as any man in this House, but what is the use of talking nonsense? Aren't you going to defend your country? What are you going to do about it? What we need is a strong voluntary system, and that you can have only by proceeding along rational lines of efficiency.

Outside the generals
named-Fiset, Ashton, MacBrien, Elmsley, Morrison, Burstall-are any other generals in Ottawa included in this vote?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No.
Outside the eleven officers of the rank of general mentioned' as being under certain military districts, are there any other generals employed by the department?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There is the commandant of the Royal Military College, General Macdonnell. Then there is a brigadier-general whose rank is only that of a colonel in the militia, General McNaughton.
What pay and allowances does he draw?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: He gets the pay of a director on the staff
Are there any other brigadier-generals?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: One in Kingston,whom I mentioned.

Are there any others,
either in the districts or in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I understand not.

I fear that the gallant member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) has rather misinterpreted my motives in the few remarks I made a moment ago. I am disposed to agree with him that none of us are enamoured of militarism. I hope he did not think I was; in fact, my remarks would rather tend the other way. I am sorry that the gallant member made reference to the talking of nonsense, for I was simply asking for information. I professed to know a little about public opinion in this country, because there have been expressions of opinion-throughout the whole of Canada, I have no doubt-in the press and otherwise, referring to the establishment of the League of Nations and expressing the hope, entertained on the part of all classes of the people in this country and throughout the world, that if the League of Nations does not succeed

in putting an end to war during the lifetime of most of us, it will do so during the lifetime of our children. I am not so sure that that will he the effect, but I am sure of this, Mr. Chairman; that following upon the Great War through which the world has so lately passed, the feelings of the people have been so shocked that they are drawing as far away as possible from the idea of war. My own idea is that the Government should fall in line with the sentiment which actuates the people and spend as little on war services as possible -spend the minimum, not the maximum amount. I believe that that is the public sentiment in Canada to-day. When I rose I desired to get an opinion from the minister whether there was not some way in which the militia expenditures could be decreased by reducing the number of officers in districts through the enlargement of some districts and the abolition of others. I believe that no one in this House or out of it who knows me would have the temerity to accuse me of not being willing to stand in the defence of my country. I feel that I am actuated by patriotic and loyal sentiments, and while the indirect reflection which the gallant colonel (Mr. Peck) evidently intended to make is resented, it is not bitterly resented, because I could see in the fervour of the gallant soldier that spirit which would naturally be characteristic of an heroic man who had come out of the greatest Armageddon that the world has ever known. While I appreciate his bravery and his prowess and the signal honours that have been bestowed upon him, I as a civilian and representing a constituency of this country, having regard to the times and the conditions, not forgetting the great debt with which we are burdened, felt it was my duty at least to suggest to the minister that he might bring his mind to bear upon the Militia Estimates in such a way as to save money to the country if possible, at the same time amply providing for the country's defence and ensuring that worthy men at present in the service should be cared for in the case of any reduction in the district staffs. On the whole, I think the adoption of any such course would save the country many hundreds of thousands of dollars yearly.
How much, approximately, is paid to these nineteen generals?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: For the districts, $66,000; and at the headquarters, $44,000.

The total vote for pay of staff is $265,000, so there would remain for

other officers of the staff who are not fortunate enough to be generals, the sum of $155,000. Included in the vote is there any allowance for travelling, for services, for batmen or messengers?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: No. This is a consolidated rate, it includes all the items except necessary travelling expenses which are in a transportation item.
Then I am to take it that this $11,000 is for the pay of generals, and the remaining $165,000 is for pay of officers below the rank of generals?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.

How many of these
officers are subalternsi?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No subalterns on the
staff.
How many captains?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No captains on the
staff.
How many majors?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Eight or ten majors.

Therefore, of the fifty
officers, we have, roughly, 19 generals, 8 majors, and the remainder are colonels?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Lieutenant-colonels.

Lieutenant-colonels, or
colonels. Would it not be possible for the minister to carry on the administration of the headquarters staff at Ottawa and the headquarters staffs in the various districts, without having so many highly paid, high-ranked officers? Some of my hon. and gallant friends on the other side,
I think, will be able to tell the minister that, while those generals and other high officers are very useful, while we practically must have them, really a large proportion of the work of the army has been done by subalterns and other officers below the rank of lieutenant-colonel and colonel. They will also be able to tell him, I think, that an officer holding the rank of colonel could carry on just as well the duties of the position of head of a military district as an officer holding the rank of general. The minister knows as well as I do that an army in the field-which is where an army should be, and is, in its greatest state of efficiency-an army of one division of fighting men of some eighteen or twenty thousand rifles, would not have anything near -the number of generals which this small permanent army of ours of 3,800 men has. It is an anomaly to be able to handle a fighting force of 18,000 to 20,000

men with perhaps five, six or, at most, ten generals, while to carry on the administration of a force of 3,800 men who, whatever may be their abilities in war time, are certainly not fighting nor carrying on the arduous duties of their profession, eighteen or nineteen generals and as many more lieutenant-colonels and colonels are required. The whole administration is apparently confided to the most highly paid officers. My hon. and gallant friends opposite know that the last war was called a subalterns' war. If subalterns were able to carry on the fighting, they should have some share in the fruits of victory and the spoils of war when they return.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I would admit at a
glance that in the higher ranks we have more than one would ordinarily expect in regard to our staff. As I am sure my hon. friend (Mr. Power) wil realize, this is a result of the war. Many
5 p.m. of these men formerly occupied junior ranks, and during or as a result of the war, they have risen and now they have senior rank. The appropriation which we ask for the staff is a modest one, not very much more than it was before the war, and $80,000 less than it was last year. That is a pretty serious cut in the staff. I have endeavoured to cut out every office possible in that staff, and I have succeeded in cutting out a number of them. The result is an appropriation of $80,000 less than that of last year and not much more than was paid under the Liberal administration when they did not have these high officers.

The minister has repeatedly, in answering arguments from this side, stated that he is not spending much more than was spent under the Liberal regime. It is not an answer to me to tell me what the Liberal administration did. I am under the impression that they spent far too much.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That may be.
I am sure we are spending far too much, because the danger has been removed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
What was spent under the Liberal regime was according to the good sense of the country in those days, and they were fair-minded men. I am using that as a comparison. There has been a tremendous increase in rent, salaries and the like, but there has not been a tremendous increase in the staff appropriation. You have the high officers entitled to the higher pay, it is true, and they have earned their
promotion in the hardest school in which they could earn it. Ordinarily, or before the war, there were only one or two or, perhaps, three of the rank of general at headquarters. To-day there are more, and the men whom we have there are, by reason of their experience in the war, the most experienced and capable men who have ever administered the militia of Canada. It is not fair for my hon. friend to say that we have nineteen generals to administer the affairs of 3,800 men. That is the least part, about twenty per cent of their work; seventy-five or eighty per cent is the administration of the militia of Canada. I think comparatively few of the Permanent Force officers devote themselves to work of that kind.
We have more generals in the militia force.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: There are some retired ones. Rank has been conferred upon them. But this does not cost the country anything. It is a high and honourable distinction, and if it is a matter of no expense to the country, no great objection should be taken to it. The administration of the militia in the various districts scattered throughout the country costs money and takes time. The work of the staff in connection with the Permanent Force is less than one-quarter of the actual work or the actual time of the staff.
Who is president of the Militia Council?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The minister.
The vice-president of the Militia Council is the deputy minister?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
What salary does the vice-president of the Militia Council receive as such, and is that additional to the salary that he receives as deputy minister?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It is additional. He is a major-general on the staff, and for that he receives $4,500. Under the law passed by this Parliament, he is seconded for duty as deputy minister, but he is entitled to his pay as major-general on the staff.
Are any other staff officers in receipt of any pay or emolument outside of that contained as their salaries in this item?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I do not think any of them have any-other emolument whatsoever, unless it is private funds.
How long has the position of vice-president of the Militia Council been held by the deputy minister? Was it formerly held by another officer?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It has been held by the deputy minister since 1906.
How many colonels are there in district No. 6 at Halifax?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Lieutenant-Colonel Anderson, General Staff Officer, and Colonel Sharpies, assistant adjutant and quartermaster-general. These are the only two, I am informed.	,
Do they both receive the same salary?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence

speechtext:
In reply to a question I asked the minister when his Estimates were before the House last, as to why Military District No. 12 had not been disbanded, I was informed that Saskatchewan had proved to 'be such a good recruiting ground, and further, his answer contained the implication that while we might not have now any military barracks, training areas, rifle ranges, or anything of that sort, the day would come when we would have these things in Saskatchewan. I have risen for the purpose of telling the minister that the people of Saskatchewan do not want them. I am sure of that. It does not matter how frequently hon. and gallant members on the Government side rise in their places and attempt to cast a stigma on hon. gentlemen on this side who wish to express their views on these questions just as conscientiously as hon. gentlemen on the other side-and I believe, with more public opinion behind them-I say it does not matter whether I as an individual be charged with cowardice and have epithets hurled at me by these hon. gentlemen. I say that when hon. and gallant members stand in their places and hurl epithets at individuals on this side, (as has been done on two occasions) that in itself is an indication of the militaristic spirit. It is that spirit that I, speaking for the people of this country object to.
I maintain with the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) that the moneys we are asked to vote here are not going for the defence of our country, as is claimed by the hon. and gallant member, but for the purpose of paying, in many instances, fat salaries to parasites. The Department of Militia and Defence is not productive. We are asked to spend about $11,750,000 for the Department of Militia and Defence. Com-
pare that with the $4,500,000 or $4,750,000 that we are spending on agriculture. Agriculture is productive. We have no honourary colonels receiving fat salaries in agriculture. I ..j&tand in my place here and say a few words to the best of my ability in the interests of agriculture, and I would like to know how much sympathy agriculture has received in this House. I would like to see hon. gentlemen stand up for the interests of agriculture, instead of urging us to vote this $11,750,000 for the Department of Militia and Defence, while agriculture goes begging. We have the wrong perspective as a people. If this money were for the purpose of providing training grounds and things of that nature, it might not he so bad; and if, as my hon. friend from Quebec South has pointed out, only the number of officers actually required to train the men were engaged, I would not be so antagonistic; but I must protest against voting large sums of money -and I gave the figures to prove it the last time I spoke-for salaries for men who walk around in an almost Prussian manner, brushing people off the sidewalk. That is the spirit of militarism that this country is asked to pay for, and it is against that spirit that I as an individual protest. I am sorry that we have men who approve of that sort of thing.

If my hon. friend is alluding to me-or if he is not, I will say it anyway. I never said anything that reflected in any shape or form on any hon. gentleman opposite, and I think hon. gentlemen opposite will bear me out when I say that since I entered this House I have never said anything to hurt the feelings of any one. I have never had any such intention and I hope that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould) who is a younger member than I, although I am pretty young myself, will moderate his language more when he speaks of the gallant men who rendered such great services in this great war and who are now in our military organization. It does not become hon. members in this House to reflect on them. They are carrying on what they were trained to do, and they are doing it well. As far as I am concerned, I do not think 1 used intemperate language. I think probably the hon. gentleman lives in a glass house in that respect.

I would like to say in reply to the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Gould's) remarks that I was a little surprised to find him objecting to high salaries. I

thought the paying of high salaries was something that was approved by the particular cult to which he belongs; because I believe the head of the organization to which he owes allegiance is receiving a salary of some $15,000 odd a year.

It is going up all the time;-$18,000 to a gentleman who does not seem to think it is worth while to spend a little while in this House in advocating the rights and interests of the farmers of this country. It comes with mighty bad grace from my hon. friend from Assini-boia (Mr. Gould) to read anybody a lecture for lack of interest in the farmers of this country, when the leader of the Farmers' party spends less time in this House than any other member of the House.

Does he go
home every week-end?

In regard to hurling epithets across the floor, of which the hon. member complains, who was the first to start that? The hon. member for Assini-boia was the first to stand on his feet in this House some days ago, and with a view solely to making a little cheap capital for himself, charge that there was a militarist party in this country-a charge which has no foundation whatever. There is no militaristic spirit in-Canada; there has not been any militaristic spirit in Canada. As the hon. and gallant member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) very properly said, you could not arouse or create a militaristic spirit in this country in the course of a century or more. What object had the hon. member for Assiniboia in getting up in this House a few days ago and trying to represent to the people of this country that there was a set of men in this House who, regardless of the interests of the people, were trying to drive us in a military direction? His object was as I stated a moment ago simply to create for himself a little cheap political capital, to give the impression in his part of the country, where I suppose he would send his speech, that the members on this side of the House were extravagant and reckless in their expenditure of money, particularly for military purposes, and that the people there could thank God a man had been discovered in Assiniboia to come down here and plead the rights of the people and to advocate economy. That was his whole object. The hon. member and certain other hon. members have not discussed the militia items, or other items that have been before the committee, on their merits; they have talked simply with the idea of creating the idea,-an absolutely false idea-throughout the country that we on this side are not actuated by motives of economy. The hon. member has no reason to make complaints about any expressions regarding members on the other side. He was himself the first to make charges that have no foundation in fact, using such terms as "Prussianism" and applying them directly or indirectly to members on this side. Those epithets, whether the hon. gentleman realises the fact or not, are insulting, and I say that his reflections have been absolutely unwarranted and have been actuated, in my humble estimation, by a desire on his part to obtain for himself a little cheap notoriety in the section of the country from which he comes.

In reference to the statements of the member for Skeena (Mr. Peck), it seems to me that there is an attempt to draw some comparison in value, if I may say so, between the individual who wears the khaki and the man who does not, who is engaged in the supposedly menial work of agriculture. Now, I want hon. gentlemen to show some sense of equity and equality. Because an officer has gone to the war and won his laurels, that is no reason why the private, who did just as much, should be asked to suffer undue taxation in order that the general may go around at ease. My complaint is that we have too many men of that rank, and the moneys that we are asked to vote for the purpose of keeping these gentlemen walking around the country doing no actual good, can be used to better advantage. The revenues of the country will not stand this burden. I say that the private man, the man who produces, the tiller of the soil, served his country during the war, in producing those things without which we could not have carried on, and he should not be called upon to provide the means of enabling these men of rank to remain idle. "Peace hath her victories no less renowned than war"; and the producer is entitled to some credit as well as the fighter. We have no emoluments to throw away, and no moneys to expend on anything that is not absolutely essential.

It is rather difficult to follow the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould), and to find out just what he wants. He began by stating that he spoke
- COMMONS
for the people of Saskatchewan, and concluded with the declaration that he spoke for the people of Canada; and in that speech he asserts that there is no need whatever for this staff, and that the defence of the country-[DOT]
I rise to a point of order. I did not make the statement that we had no desire whatever for the staff.
Will the hon. member say what he does mean?
I made the statement that we had too many men of this kind, and I stand by that statement. I did not say, however, that we had no desire whatever for the staff.
Does the hon. member know how many staff officers there are in the district from which he comes?
I can get the figures.

The hon. gentleman has, on several occasions, confessed that he does not know anything about the subject, but he usually proceeds to tell us all about it. He complains about the size of the staff in the district from which he comes, and when I ask him what is its size he says he does not know. Well, that is a fair indication of his knowledge of the whole subject. Now, the creation of a staff is a matter of a lifetime. The securing of suitable men takes years, and any man who knows anything about the matter knows how much work is involved in gathering a proper staff. In agriculture, I believe, there is an organization to which the member for Assiniboia belongs, and the chief of that organization draws $18,000 a year from it, and $4,000 a year from this House.
I rise to a point of order. The hon. member is now speaking on a subject of which he is ignorant. The president of the association to which he refers does not receive five cents of a salary.
There is not an organization in this country-
A point of order has been raised.
The point of order is not well taken.

There is not an organization, whether commercial, industrial, or agricultural, that has not a staff to lead and direct its operations. The leader

of the American Federation of Labour is a high-salaried man, and I was reading the other day that the leader of the Boilermakers' Union gets $15,000 a year. The Great War Veterans' Association has a staff that is almost as highly paid as a military staff; and the Manufacturers' Association has a staff which is also very well paid. There is not a body of men in the country, I repeat, that has not a highly paid staff of men carefully selected to direct its operations. If I were asked to say what items should be wiped out, I would leave the item of staff to the last. Because you can raise an army of men in six months, you can get officers in two years, and commanding officers in five years, but you cannot get a staff under twenty years. When the hon. gentleman, who does not know the strength of the staff in his district, proposes that that staff should be reduced because it is too numerous, I think we have a fair intimation of just what he does know, and we can properly appraise the advice which he proffers.
In reference to district 12, what do they pay for rent in connection with the staff in the city of Regina?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That question does not arise under this vote, but I shall furnish my hon. friend with the particulars on another occasion.

If I understood the member for Assiniboia rightly, he said that they lacked accommodation in Saskatchewan in connection with armouries or drill halls. We have an armoury in the city of Moose jaw which would be a credit to any place, being on a par with practically ^ny of the armouries that have been built; it cost over $100,000. If I am correctly informed, in Regina the minister is paying rent for all the space he occupies there. This splendid building in the city of Moosejaw is absolutely idle the year round, although a man has to be kept there to take care of it, and hundreds of tons of coal are consumed in the winter to keep the place heated and in condition. There is ample office accommodation and room for training there. There are five acres of land in connection with this institution, and floor space that will accommodate some 6,000 persons. Yet, the place stands absolutely idle from one year's end to the other, while the minister is paying right along for space in the other city where he has a staff.
Is there a permanent veterinary officer at Halifax?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I understand that we have no veterinary officer at Halifax now.
Is it intended to appoint one?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Not to appoint an additional one. It may be that some of the present staff may be moved, but I do not think it likely they would go to Halifax. I doubt if there are enough horses there to occupy their attention. You could get part-time men to attend to them for there are only some sixteen or twenty horses there.

I was quite interested
indeed in the remarks made by the hon. member for Assiniboia, particularly in that part of his speech where he said he spoke for the people of Saskatchewan. I do not know where he got his authority to speak, for instance, for the constituency of Regina. I am of the opinion that I was elected to represent those people, and that I am the person who is supposed to speak for them. More than that, I have not a committee of fifteen in the constituency of Regina to tell me what I am to do. The hon. gentleman seems to think that the people of Saskatchewan are opposed to the existence of a military body in Canada-that is the so-called militia such as is now being organized and which has always existed in the Dominion. Such an impression I have found to be entirely incorrect. I do know this, that quite recently it was suggested that Military District No. 12, which covers the entire province of! Saskatchewan, should be disbanded and merged with some other district, and I want to say to my hon. friend that at no time during the four years I have represented the constituency of Regina have I been appealed to as strongly as I have recently to try and induce the Government not to disband that district. The Minister of Militia will admit that I made as strong representations to him as possible not to do so. Our people by the dozen appealed to me. They met in bodies, and represented to me that it would be a very unpopular and very unwise thing to disband that district; they wished to continue the militia organization in the interest of the defence of Canada, knowing the advantage it was when the war broke out. When the war began-my hon. friend may not know it; probably he was just harvesting wheat and doing nothing else at that time; probably he has done nothing 177
else but harvest wheat since, I do not know -our people took a very active interest in military matters, and they have continued to do so from that day until now. They know the advantage of the militia system; they know that our men rallied immediately to the colours to support the militia we had there. They know more than that-they know that out there our farmers' sons enlisted until in some districts there was not a single farmer's son left to attend to the farm duties. I hope that in the district where my hon. friend comes from they had a similar spirit. I do not know that they had, but I do know that was the feeling in our part of the country. I know this further: that as a result of that our farmers to-day are desirous that in the constituency of Regina-and I can speak for no more, although I will admit that more than one-half of the correspondence I am attending to here comes from districts represented by the Farmers' party which seems very funny to me when the people are said to be so satisfied with the representatives; but I am not speaking for them and not attempting to-I do know that the people in the constituency that I represent, both in the urban and rural districts, think the militia organization should be continued, not for militaristic purposes, but for the purposes of defence as it existed before.
Now, the attitude taken by our farmer friends here seems very strange to me. We find the hon. member for Assiniboia evidently opposing anything in the way of military expenditure. Then the gentleman who is evidently leading that party to-day, the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) lives, I believe, in Moosejaw, and as soon as he sees a chance to get the military organization up into Moosejaw, where it might be of some local advantage to him, he suggests to the minister that the organization be moved there. Now, I take this attitude as a citizen of Canada-that if any department can be managed more economically and better from any other city I am not going to press the claim of the city of Regina. But the general opinion is that the capital of a province is the proper place for such a headquarters to be, and I think investigation will prove that to be the case. It seems very strange to me that as soon as it comes to a question of the interest of the pants pockets of persons in the constituency where the hon. gentlemen of the Farmers' party live then they forget all about their principles.

I made no reference
whatever to the removal of the district

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: headquarters, I merely drew attention to the fact that there was a $140,000 or $150,000 building now standing absolutely empty, that is quite suitable for the accommodation of the staff not only of the military district in question but of the entire Dominion as far as space is concerned. That building is standing absolutely idle while rent is being paid for quarters for this staff in the city which my hon. friend who has just taken his seat represents. I am not concerned with the moving of the -district at all, but I am concerned that a building of that character should stand idle while we as taxpayers are paying rent for property in other places. It is purely a matter of economy with me. Personally I am of opinion we might do away with several of the districts, and I would ask the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) to give us the benefit of his opinion. I would ask him if he does not think that Military District No. 12, which is now located at Regina, could very well serve the purposes of the provinces on either side of it. We have the military district for the province of Alberta located at Calgary, up near the mountains, almost in the extreme west of that province. In the province of Manitoba, on the other side there is another military district. When military training was required the troops were brought down to Camp Hughes for that purpose. And yet there is a spacious building in the province of Saskatchewan roomy enough to accommodate the staffs of these other districts. It seems strange to me that we should have three military districts when one located at a central point, in the way I have explained, would be just as convenient for the three provinces concerned.

Are you of opinion that if all the troops in these provinces were trained at Camp Hughes the extra cost df moving those troops would be more than met by the saving affected by the combination of the districts?

I am not expressing an
opinion at all, I am asking for an opinion. I do not pretend to know anything about the subject except that the training of all the troops in the West was done at Camp Hughes.
During the war?
Yes.
We are not training for war now, it is a peace training we are providing for.

Where is the annua;
training being done?

At local headquarters and at camps. Calgary is the camp for Alberta, and the local headquarters in wherever the local unit is. The local units are training at local headquarters this year and not travelling at all.

The remarks of the hon.
member for Maple Creek evidently indicate that, while the war was on, his thoughts were not on the struggle at all but on the conduct of his farm and the profits to be derived therefrom-nothing else. If he knew anything at all about the subject he would not have made the statement he did to-day, that our troops were trained at Camp Hughes. At the beginning of the war they did train there, but if he had taken any interest in the subject at all he would know that while the war was in progress a new district, known as Military District No. 12, was created, and that the troops in that district were trained in the exhibition camp in Regina. I know that because I was in the camp for more than two years. If the hon. gentleman was paying any attention to the conduct of the war, and especially to the preparations being made in his own province, he ought to know that; if he doesn't know it he ought not to talk about it at all.

I think the hon. member is wandering away from the subject by indulging in these personalities. It is just possible that I know as much about the war, and had as many anxious thoughts over it, as the hon. member who has just sat down. That was not my purpose in rising, for I would be the last one to bring in anything like that, but the hon. member must have his little personal flings. I am not taking second place to anyone so far as the war is concerned, and it would be as well for the hon. member to have his own skirts absolutely clean before he criticises the skirts of other people.
The hon. member for Maple Creek did me the honour to direct a question to me with regard to the organization.
Correct.

I believe in the principle of de-centralization. I do not believe you could administer the whole militia force of Canada through the general staff any more than you could govern the provinces through this Parliament. The division in the Prairie Provinces does not necessarily follow along geographical lines, and taking

into consideration the number of militia regiments I think it would be most unwise to reduce the districts there. In that particular I may quote the opinion of oui greatest soldier, General Sir Arthur Currie, who, having gone very thoroughly intc this question, reached the conclusion that it would be impossible to reduce the military districts without great detriment to the force.

I think the eommitee is at sea in trying to find the exact truth. We have had expression of widely divergent opinions from the hon. member for Regina and the hon. member for Maple Creek. But there is a gentleman here who has a wide knowledge of Western Canada, and in particular of the riding of Moosejaw-I would like to hear the Minister of Immigration give us his views as to the exact truth in respect of this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, for some time there has been considerable discussion regarding the location of headquarters in Military District No. 12. The matter has been thoroughly discussed by the Militia Department and its officers, and" after very careful consideration of all the factors they reached the decision that military headquarters should be made in the city of Regina. So far as I am concerned, I abide by the decision of those gentlemen, and the minister apparently concurs in their conclusion. With reference to the other point mentioned by the member for Maple Creek, that is, the advisability of using one of these large armouries as offices for headquarters staff, I understand they were never built for that purpose, but solely for military drill, and very material alterations would be necessary to adapt them for office purposes.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Permanent Force, $6,255,000.

Before this item carries
I should like to have obtained considerable information from the minister, but the time before six o'clock is too short. To bring the matter to a head, I move for the reduction of this Estimate by the sum of $2,000,000. In support of this reduction I argue as follows:	We are asking for
this large amount of $6,255,000 to maintain a Permanent Force, that is, a force of men who could all the year round be in uniform and be trained for warlike purposes. The force amounts in all to 3,800 men. The amount required to pay them at $1,75 per day-in contradistinction to the $1.10
177J
which the private soldier was paid during the war-would 'be $2,429,000.

What about the
officers ?

I am coming to them in
a moment. To board those soldiers would require something like $1,000,000, so that we would have to set apart about $3,500,000 for their pay and board. Now I come to the officers. We would have over $2,000,000 left to pay the officers. We have already paid nineteen generals and twenty-five or thirty colonels $265,000, and we are told that their duty consists in looking after this force. I fail to see why we should be called upon to pay an extra $2,000,000 to them. But, lest I be accused of preaching as a demagogue, I will give a further reason. Our Permanent Force of 3,800 men represents, roughly, one man for every mile of the boundary line which divides us from our neighbours to the south. The Minister of Militia the other evening stated that he had cut down his Estimates to the lowest possible figure consistent with safety. When I asked him what danger he anticipated, he was unable to tell me. I am forced to conclude that the only danger he sees is the danger of aggression from our neighbour to the south. If he thinks 3,800 men are sufficient to defend us from that quarter, any soldier in the House will tell him that one man per mile is not sufficient. If this force is for training purposes-and I presume this is its principal purpose-I submit that we do not need to train soldiers at the present moment, for we have 400,000 of the best soldiers in the world that only two years ago returned from fighting in the greatest of all wars. They have learned how to fight on the bitterest of all fields, and they have become efficient enough to earn encomiums from the nations of the world. I do not say that as time goes on and these men disappear we will not have to replace them, and that we will not have to go in for further military training, but I submit that at the present moment, when we have no enemy either near or far to face, when, even if we had, we have a stronger and better disciplined and more efficient fighting organization in our returned men than we have ever in our history, when this organization can be called together in a matter of weeks to face any foe,-there is no necessity to incur this heavy military expenditure.

Why does my hon. friend limit his cut to two millions? Why

does he not move that the whole item be eliminated?
I limited the reduction to two millions because it was supposed to be necessary to have the skeleton of an army in case of any sudden uprising.

My hon. friend is
arguing that there is no such necessity.

I argue that for the present there is no great necessity; if my hon. friend will bqck me up, of course, I will move to cut out the whole thing. If I cannot get his consent to that I would ask him to go with me a little way in that direction.
I feel very highly flattered to think that my hon. friend's judgment on military matters should be so influenced.

My judgment in all matters in connection with parliamentary affairs is influenced a great deal by the way my hon. friend expresses himself and the way he votes. Ever, since I came into this House I have followed his speeches and his views and his votes with considerable attention and have governed myself accordingly. For a number of years I have been endeavouring to obtain better treatment for the widowed mothers of soldiers. I am told that approximately $2,000,000 a year would well look after this class of our people who suffered through the war. I prefer that this $2,000,000 should be spent in this way rather than to train people to begin another war. My view is that before we embark on any further warlike or belligerent undertakings we should pay our debts to those who suffered as a result of the last war. Let us see that the widows and orphans of those who laid down their lives obtain something which shall prevent them from having to scrape in order to earn a living. If hon. gentlemen opposite do not wish to spend this money, through pensions and re-establishment, for the benefit of the widows and orphans, it could be devoted to the relief of the distress caused by unemployment and to look after the returned soldiers who so gallantly fought in the great war. If we did this we would alleviate in some degree the unrest and the bitter feeling which prevails among the returned men who since coming back to Canada have felt that promises made to them during the war were made only to be broken. I move, Mr. Chairman, that this item be reduced by $2,000,000.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This item is reduced by a quarter of a million from the amount voted last year. It provides now for 4,000 rank and file and 412 officers, at ah average of $1,350 each. My hon. friend's calculation is very wide of the mark. He has taken the basis of the pay of a private soldier only as a first-year man. He has allowed nothing for non-commissioned officers, nothing for the 950 horses we have to maintain, nothing for thirty or forty other items which he has not mentioned. We have already cut this item to the bone. In fact, unless there are some desertions during the summer, we may be just a little short. But in the hot weather there are always a certain number of desertions, and allowing for these the item will suffice, I trust, for the present fiscal year.
Where and in what numbers are the men of the Permanent Force now stationed?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The following is a list of the military districts with the number of men at each: No. 1, London, 261; No. 2, Toronto, 580; No. 3, Kingston, 435; No. 4, Montreal, 321; No. 5, Quebec, 463; No. 6, Halifax, 664; No. 7, St. John, 82; No. 10, Winnipeg, 512; No. 11, Victoria, 409; No. 12, Regina, 63; No. 13, Calgary, 210.
Amendment (Mr. Power) negatived; yeas, 37, nays, 60.

Is it the intention of the Government to reduce the number of the mounted police? We were told last year that either one or the other system would be adopted, that of the mounted police or that of the standing militia, as a Permanent Force for Canada. Is the Mounted Police Force to be continued or reduced, and is the militia to be continued and increased?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Provision was made a
year ago for an establishment of some 2,500 members in the Mounted Police force. As a matter of fact, if I am not mistaken, we have not exceeded 1,800. The Main Estimates this year will provide for in the neighbourhood of about 1,600 men to be retained in the Mounted Police, and it is proposed to carry that force for at least this year.

We were told by the Government last year, in passing the Main Estimates for the Mounted Police, that they had not determined whether they would retain a Mounted Police force sufficient to replace the militia, or whether they would

adopt the policy of maintaining the militia and reducing the Mounted Police. Has any conclusion been come to by the Government as to which of these two forces they are going to perpetuate and to increase and which they are to decrease.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The services are different. It has been decided that for this year we shall maintain the Mounted Police force in Eastern and Western Canada with an establishment of about 1,600 men. The question whether the Mounted Police force is to continue indefinitely has not been determined.

Have the Government received from provincial governments protests as to the establishment of this Mounted Police force and their activities in the several provinces of Canada? If so, from what provinces have protests been received?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That question is hardly in order on these Estimates.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the committee that it would be out of order to go into any lengthy discussion of the Estimates of the Mounted Police on the Militia Estimates. The Mounted Police, as every one well knows, are under the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Calder). When his Estimates are before the committee, these questions will, of course, be quite in order.

I do not wish to start a discussion which would be out of order.' I would not have put my question to the Minister of Militia; but when I saw his colleague, the President of the Council, taking part in the debate, I thought the question which I put was in order on account of his having intervened. So long as the Minister of Militia will conduct the discussion, I will not press my question; but if the President of the Council wishes to take part in the discussion, I think my question is perfectly in order.
