Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Before the House resumes in Committee of Supply, Mr. Speaker,-this is not a motion-I desire, with your permission, to say, in regard to the question put by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon, as to what hours will he observed commencing Monday, that the Government is of opinion that we should observe the practice of last session and conform to city time, so that there may be no confusion.

The House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the Committee rose at 6 o'clock the Estimates of Militia and Defence were under consideration. The committee had reached item No. 102 on page 30 of the Estimates. This item -had been considered and an amendment had been moved and disposed of. Shall the item now carry?

At six o'clock I was addressing a question to the Government regarding the strength of the Permanent Force, and I desire now to quote briefly from certain remarks made by the minister in charge of the Mounted Police Estimates last year, in which he discussed military items. He said:
With reference to the future of the force, here is the question with which we are faced. It is essential to maintain a police force for certain purposes. It is essential to maintain it for the Yukon and Northwest Territories. It is necessary to have a federal police for certain im-
(Mr. Cannon.]
portant purposes that the federal police have served during all these years. In addition we must have some force as a reserve for the main-tainence of law and order. We can choose between having a permanent military force of a certain strength which the Government might consider adequate to our needs in Canada, or of preserving this force at a substantial strength. I do not think any member of the House will say that we should have no force in Canada. We must have some force. The question is whether it is wiser to have a military force of a greater strength or to have a smaller . military force and keep up the Mounted Hoi ice for the purposes of a reserve force, as well as for performing the necessary police duties.
My own personal view is that it is better to have a larger Mounted Police Force and a smaller military force than we otherwise would require. Hon. members may not agree with that but that is my view and that is the view that the Government has acted upon. Another Government might reach a different conclusion. It might consider it desirable to make this force a part of the Permanent Military Force. We did at one time discuss that proposal but we came to the conclusion that the Mounted Police is a better force for preserving law and order than either the militia or the Permanent Force.
Now, I wish to ask the Government whether they have come to any conclusion with regard to the references made to .the different forces by the minister who had charge of the Mounted Police Estimates last year-whether the military force is to he increased by a strength that would be deemed sufficient and the Mounted Police Force eliminated or reduced, or whether it is the intention to maintain the two forces more or less independently of each other rather than amalgamate them, as was suggested by the minister last year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I may say in answer
to the question that there are two opinions upon that subject. I know the opinion of Sir Arthur Currie, when Inspector-General of the Forces of Canada, was that there should be but one department of defence in this country, and that it should embrace not only the military but also the Naval, Air and Mounted Police Force. His opinion was that the whole of our defence scheme should be under one department. However, another opinion is prevalent upon that question. That is that we require a force in Canada more particularly detailed for police work than is the lot of any military force that I know of in this country or in any other country-that is such work as has been done for a great many years by the mounted police of our northwestern country. That is essentially police work-the maintenance of law and order being one branch of the force, the ferreting out and discovery of crime being another branch of it and the general administra-

tion of criminal law which is largely entrusted in our western provinces to that organization. However, in the results this arrangement has been reached-that instead of increasing our military force we have determined to keep it down to less than half the amount authorized, and at the same time our proposal is to decrease the Mounted Police Force. As the minister stated this afternoon the force last year was approximately 1,800 men. This year he proposes to reduce it to 1,600 men, with a corresponding reduction of about a million dollars in expenditure. It is felt that at present we had better proceed on the old lines, keeping the police as a civil force distinct from the military force. Of course, I do not know what the ultimate result may be in the years to come, but personally I was very much influenced by the opinion of Sir Arthur Currie upon the subject. So far as I can speak at the present time, the determination of the Government is to maintain the two forces but at largely reduced strength to that authorized.

The minister does not
state definitely that any policy has been arrived at?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The policy is the one
that I have stated-to maintain them as distinct forces at greatly reduced numbers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Is it intended to construct
any new barracks this year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
We are badly in need
of barracks, Mr. Chairman, but we do not feel that we would be warranted in incurring the expenditure at the present time. We are also badly in need of drill accommodation for some of the militia units, but that matter will have to stand to a future date.

The Royal Mounted
Police used to be stationed at Ottawa, are they here still?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Personally, I do not
really know. There are Mounted Police here, but I am not familiar with their numbers.
Are there detachments of the Royal Mounted Police stationed elsewhere than in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes, at several points, but I am not really familiar with them. I know there are police at Winnipeg, Vancouver, Regina, and I think possibly at Edmonton also. There are 1,600 scattered at various points.

What work do they
do in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am not very familiar with the answer to that question. I know they do guard the public buildings, they have taken the place of the old Dominion police, but I am really not well enough informed on the matter to say.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As I ruled before
six o'clock, I think any discussion on the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, or the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as the body is now called, would be more properly in order on the Estimates of the minister in charge of that body, that is the hon. the President of the Privy Council.
Mr. D'ANJOU (Rimouski) :	(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I wish to register my protest, as I have always done year after year, against military expenditures, before the passing of this item by the parliamentary majority. In fact, the necessity has never been so urgent in this country of ours as at the present time to practise the strictest economy in every way possible.
Our military expenses, during the last war, ran up to a very high figure, and, as it has often been said, that war was fought in order to prevent further conflicts. Then we have the League of Nations which was established with a view to settling disputes between the various countries of the world. This league is costing us quite a lot of money and I think the time has come when the Government should realize that our military expenditure must necessarily be cut down to the lowest possible figure. It is the duty of the Government to devote their efforts to peaceful undertakings, instead of voting money for armouries and military drill halls. They should rather attend to the building of agricultural schools and experimental farms and the establishment of demonstration plots. I, for one, would be ready to support any appropriation to that effect, but I do object to any superfluous military expenditure.
In the course of the debate, last night, the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. McCurdy) asked for a vote of $25,000 to build a drill hall in the Maritime Provinces. We objected to that item and I believe we acted in the public interest. When hon. members ask the. Government to vote some money for agricultural or other very useful purposes, they are told that the financial condition, of the country does not justify such expenditure. This year the

Estimates of the Department of Agriculture amount to $4,000,000 only, while we are asked to vote nearly $12,000,000 for the Militia Department. If the Government realized their duty and should the Minister of militia be not quite so militaristic, it would be the very opposite and instead of voting twelve millions for military purposes, that money would be applied to agriculture.
At the present time there are more drill halls than agricultural schools or experimental farms in this country. I understand that the Government, such as it was asked by the Minister of Public Works yesterday may build drill halls in the constituencies whose representatives are supporters of the Administration; I understand that, on the eve of an election, a sum of $25,000 may be asked for military purposes, in order to help an hon. member who is now supporting the Government; but, in my opinion, such expenditure is absolutely unnecessary and unjustified. In view of our present financial troubles and the unrest which is prevailing throughout the country, the Government ought to cut down considerably the military expenditure and that would help us to meet the enormous obligations which we have assumed by taking part in the war. It is not soldiers that we want, but tillers of the soil. That ought to be the aim of the Government. It would be better if they endeavoured to impress upon our young men a disposition for agriculture, to better the condition of the farmer and to make life easier and more pleasant for him. That would be a much better way to help in the development of this country and in paying the enormous debt we have incurred through our foolish and hazardous experience during the last war.
No wonder that the country is facing bankruptcy. Did not Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) state, at the outbreak of the war, that he was ready" to lead the country into bankruptcy in order that we might take part in the war? His wishes have been heard and, to-day this Dominion whose Government he is now leading, is absolutely bankrupt.
Mr. Chairman, as soon as hon. members on this side get up and criticise the military and naval Estimates, they are charged by the majority of hon. members opposite with being disloyal. It has even suggested, during the present review, that hon. members who refused to give their whole support to the Minister of Marine or the Minister of Militia,

when they present their Estimates, lacked intelligence. Well, Mr. Chairman, I consider that the most intelligent members are those who realize best the interests of the country and who want this Dominion to resume its course towards its destinies.
I am absolutely opposed to this military expenditure and I said so at the last review. It is my opinion and I am here to voice my views and those of the people I have the honour to represent. I wanted very much to make these observations before the hon. minister had. the item passed by the majority surrounding him.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Royal Military College, $350,000.
How does the attendance at the college this year compare with that of other years?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The work of the Royal Military College on its military and on its civil side is gradually extending. The number of candidates in attendance during the college year just closing is one hundred and sixty-three. One hundred and two tried the examination last year. Sixty-one were successful, and of these seven did not take the college course.
What is the reason for the increase in this item over last year?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: It is largely attributable to increases granted to the civilian staff by the Civil Service Commission, who classified them and fixed their salaries. I have the particulars, but it is a very long list.
What education besides the military is given?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: A broad general education equal to the education that one receives in many of our universities. It is accepted by the various law and medical schools up to matriculation. Special courses are given in engineering and military subjects, but the ordinary classical, mathematical and English as well as French education is provided for.
Are all the students obliged to take some portion of military training even if they specialize in particular subjects?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Oh, yes, there is an
elaborate system of what I suppose I might call military gymnastics as part of the students' daily life.
Do the students get practice in gunnery.	-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: They have special exercises in gunnery, hut the actual firing practice is taken at Petawawa Camp.
What entrance examination is required?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: In Ontario we would say it is considerably higher than the entrance examination to our high schools.
What is the attendance from the various provinces?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
A few students come
from Montreal, but the attendance is largely made up from Ontario and the West, although the college is open to every part of Canada.
Is there any attempt to make the institution self-sustaining, and to what extent is it not so?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
These are the fees payable by the cadets:	First year, $400;
second year, $250; third year, $250; total, $900. That includes all fees, board, etc.
Do the students attending that college get a practical training in engineering, civil and electrical, corresponding with that given in a school of technology?	.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: A very elaborate course is given in civil engineering; there is also a course in electrical engineering. These are purely civilian courses, though they are considered as of the highest significance in connection with military training.
Are steps taken by the department or by the college itself to advertise the institution and bring it to the notice of the young men of the country?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We did advertise it very generally throughout Canada, but just at present we have withdrawn all the advertisements because we have as many cadets as we can accommodate. I did hear that the number of applicants for the next term, commencing next fall, has not reached the maximum, and some advertising may be done during this summer. The local governments are specially notified of vacancies, of the requirements, and of the curriculum, and are urged to send their full complement of students.
Is the primary purpose of the college to prepare men for officers' commissions in the Permanent Force of Canada?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
No, that is not the
object. The college was established by Hon. Alexander MacKenzie in 1874. It had a double purpose, a broad civil training and also a thorough military training. But practically no inducement is offered to cadets who pass examinations there to enter the service. I think only five commissions are offered to cadets. In former years two Imperial commissions were offered; I do not know whether that practice has been continued since the war. Just at this time the Permanent Force establishment is complete and we are not able to offer any military commissions at all.
Am I right in assuming that this item of $350,000 is what is required over and above the revenue derived from tuition fees?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The vote now asked is the total cost of the institution. Anything received from the students is paid directly to the Receiver General.

Could the minister give
the committee an idea how much the college is costing?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The total expenditure
for last year was $219,160 and the revenue was $53,598. The net expenditure chargeable to the public would be $165,561.74.

As the Royal Military College is situated in a corner of my constituency, I have naturally taken considerable interest in it, before, as well as since, I became a member of this House. Although the institution is in the county of Frontenac I do not claim it as belonging to my constituency, because in an especial sense it belongs to the whole Canadian people. I can remember, Sir, when I first entered this House and sat in Opposition, that I was impressed with the manner in which members on -both sides regarded the Royal Military College-as an institution belonging as much to the whole of the people as to the part of the country in which it happened to be situated. Members at all times have been disposed not only to take a justifiable pride in the Royal Military College, but to deal very generously with it. I need not recite the fame that has come to the college through the work done by its graduates, not only on the field of battle, where they have won undying fame for themselves, their college and their country, but in other walks of life; they have brought to the college and to the Dominion in various parts of the

world well deserved honour. The college has been particularly fortunate in the gentlemen who have from time to time occupied the position of commandant, but at no time in its history, I believe, has it been more fortunate in that respect than at the present time under the direction of General Sir Archibald Macdonnell. I need not refer to his distinguished military career; others here are more capable of doing that than I am. But I have had the privilege and the pleasure of associating more or less intimately with him, and I know that he maintains that close touch with the students which is essential to the best results in any university or college.' One cannot put a value upon close personal relationship between a man like General Sir Archibald Macdonnell and the cadets who are attending that school. The commandant also takes a very close personal interest in the advancement of the school. It is the West Point of Canada, and he has looked upon it almost as something belonging to himself. He is deeply interested in making things look presentable so that people from the United States or elsewhere who inspect the institution will be favourably impressed with our Royal Military College. In that regard I just want to throw out this hint to the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) and his colleague the Minister of Justice. The commandant wants to improve the surrpundings of the college, and, in my estimation, that could be done at a minimum of expense, if there was co-operation between the Department of Justice and the Militia Department in this respect. Just across the water, a very short distance from the Royal Military College, is that institution known also to fame, although to a different kind of fame, Portsmouth penitentiary, in which there are a number of convicts in need of exercise. At present, they obtain that exercise, in a way of doubtful benefit to many of them, by simply breaking stones. The operation of breaking stones may be made one of general public advantage if a number of these convicts from the penitentiary could be put into a launch, brought down with their guards to the Royal Military College and set to work there on the scheme which General Sir Archibald Macdonnell has in mind of building a driveway right along the lake-front so as to add very much to the general appearance of the grounds around the military college. This, it seems to me, could be done with advantage to the public and with no expense at all. Those convicts might better be employed in work

of that kind building a nice driveway around that college to beautify the grounds., than, in a shed cracking limestone from day-to-day and week-end to week-end without any return or anything to stimulate their minds or to do them any good. That is something which I have hinted at before, and which, it seems to me, might be carried out to the advantage of the institution.
I am glad to see the Government has undertaken the erection of buildings-and those buildings are now in course of erection-which will give to the college more accommodation for class-rooms than it has had in the past. I have had some little experience with college work, I mean in going through college, and I can appreciate, as I am sure every hon. member in this chamber can, who has ever attended school, what a handicap it has been to this institution in years past to have these students packed into a place not one-quarter as large as it should be. The number of cadets allowed to enter the college is limited. It is a case of first come, first served. Those who get their applications in first, will be most likely to have an opportunity of attending the college.
They have to pass an examination.

Yes. I hope to see the day when this institution will be enlarged as our means increase, as I hope they will, so that more young men can avail themselves of the splendid training that is given there. If I had a dozen sons-and I wish to goodness I had-I would certainly, if I possibly could, rake and scrape together the money to send every one of those boys for, at least, one year to the Royal Military College, if not for anything other than to get the physical training at the institution. The instruction those young men get along that line is simply marvellous. It is wonderful what they can do in that institution with a young man in the way of systematic physical training. The students have been drawn, as the mnister has stated, from all parts of the country. Some very distinguished graduates have come from Quebec. More,
9. p.m. I suppose, naturally, have come from Ontario. I do not know that the institution has received as many as it should have from the provinces down by the sea. I hope, in years to come, it will receive more students from other parts of our Dominion. I would urge upon hon. gentlemen that, if they have a week-end to spare, they visit Kingston and make a

call at the Royal Military College. I can assure them that the commandant will be delighted to have them visit the institution and that he will show them around with the very greatest of pleasure. I am sure that if they can spend a week-end in that way, they will come back feeling that the time has not been wasted.

I think I may say that I shall be one of the last to criticise any expenditure for purposes of education, and I am glad to be assured, as I have known in the past, that the Royal Military College at Kingston is a most efficient institution. I do not doubt that at all. I will say, however, that I have always been under the impression, as I think many other people have, that the purpose of the Royal Military College is more in the nature of preparing young men to enter the military service of Canada. Personally, I am rather surprised to find that- only a very small number, some five or six, are actually offered an opportunity of entering the military service, and that the greater proportion of the instruction offered and the courses presented there are for general purposes of education. I note, from what the minister has said, that it costs the country for the conduct of this college something in excess of $150,000. I am not complaining about that expenditure; but I think, under the Constitution of Canada, the British North America Act, the matter of general education is something for the provinces to deal with, and I am curious to know in what way it has come about that the Dominion of Canada is entering upon the matter of general education.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: We entered upon it many years ago.
I am trying to get the explanation.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The explanation is that it was in connection with the military system in Canada, and that was its justification. But we have broken the strict letter of our constitution in many ways in regard to education. We spend money for agricultural education, for technical education, for naval education. It is not correct to say that all education is, by our Constitutional Act, given to the provinces.

Have we any technical
schools?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
We spend money on
technical education.

We have no technical
schools. I wish we had.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think one would call the Royal Military College at Kingston a technical school in every sense of the word.
I remember arguing in this House in the early days when I brought up the first technical education proposition, that that was a good instance of a technical school.
I also argued at that time, that is fifteen or eighteen years ago now, that we spend money on educational lines which, under the strict letter of the Constitution, we should, perhaps, not do, but we have done it from Confederation down to the present time. This school was established as long ago as 1874. Our authority to establish it, or our right to carry it on, has never been seriously questioned.

To clear up a misconception in my hon. friend's mind, I may say that the education given is primarily' a military education. A military education is primarily based upon a sound general education. When the minister referred to the fact that five commissions were given, he meant to say, and I think he did say, that they were given in the Permanent Force. Every graduate of the Military College is required to serve three years in the Canadian Militia after graduation, and as a matter of fact nearly all graduates of the Military College serve in the active militia of Canada. Furthermore, all the graduates, with the exception of one or two who were physically incapacitated, served in the great war. They are required to serve in the active militia by the terms of their original engagement on joining the college.

Let me suggest to the minister three reasons which I have not heard mentioned, any one of which ought to be sufficient to pass any item relating to the Royal Military College at Kingston.
In the first place, it was established by a Liberal Government, the Government of the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie. In the second place, the education received at the Royal Military College has resulted in the turning out of most of the engineers under whom the great public works of Canada have been constructed. In the third place,, the Royal Military College at the present time is under the command of Sir Archibald Macdonnell, than whom there is no more accomplished soldier or thorough gentleman on the face of the earth today. These are three reasons which operate to mitigate my objection to militarism in any manner, shape or form and incline

me to view with favour the passing of any item relating to the Royal Military College. I just wanted to offer these observations and to corroborate all that my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has said about the present commandant, with whose friendship I have had the privilege of being honoured since we both played football together, now many years ago.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Topographic Survey, $45,000.
Does this include mapping?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.
I think that next year there should be some increase in this item. We are a hundred years behind other countries now in our mapping, and I think the service should be enlarged.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I quite agree, and I am doing the best I can to maintain this vote. All I was able to get this year was $45,000, the same as last year. I realize that the work is proceeding slowly, but I realize more, and I am advised by men most competent to advise me on the subject, that one of the most important branches of military education is mapping, and not only the making of maps but map reading.	[DOT]
Are the maps that are made based on the Geodetic Survey?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Yes.

I want to say a word in connection with the Topographic Survey.
I commend it very highly. As to the Geodetic Survey that started a few years ago, about 1908, with a very small item, something like $8,000. Last year the item was $300,000. The members of this House have received a pamphlet describing the "net" system of work of the Geodetic Survey in the province of Ontario. This system adopted by the Geodetic Survey is of no earthly value for general survey purposes. If hon. gentlemen will inquire how the geodetic survey of India was made, they will, find that the method followed was altogether different from that adopted here. This method in Canada of making a number of long triangulations called a "net" and all that sort of thing, is the worst system that could be adopted. In India they do their work by triangles formed along base lines. The head of the Geodetic Survey in Canada says that it is going to take 200 years to make the survey the way they are doing. I would suggest

that they change the method and get the work done in a few years. The Militia Ordnance Survey is operating on altogether different lines. There is no finer work done in any country, so far as topographic surveying is concerned, than by our Department of Militia, and they have been scamped for money. Half the boys have been working for nothing to get the work done. We are spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on the useless work of a geodetic survey and I think it is time the Department of Militia got more money so that they could complete a topographic survey at least of the provinces that lie along the border. In British Columbia they are carrying on a topographic survey in connection with the Dominion Mines Department, and their work is far in advance of the work in any other country. They are doing it by means of the camera. The specimens of their work that have been published by the Department of Mines are quite equal to anything done by the Mines Department in the United States. I just wanted to call the attention of the House to that wasteful item of $300,000 for puting a few pyramids here and there and triangulating for miles across without any apparent start, or any apparent finish, or any real object. Any one who wants to learn about the geodetic survey work done in the British Empire can see a fine example of it in India. In Canada those who are doing this work do not understand anything at all about it, and yet we are spending such a vast sum of money on something of no value. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) remembers very well when he and I spoke in 1909 in favour of a geodetic survey.
I never dreamt then that we were going to spend years putting a net work of triangulation across the country from Ottawa that is not of any use. If anybody wants to get an idea of geodetic survey work, and how it should be done, he can find out in ten minutes by consulting the Encyelopaadia Britannica under "surveying," and he will find out from reading that article and then reading the report describing the work done by the Geodetic Survey in Canada, that the work done here is of no earthly use to us, and is not in accordance with any system in the world except that of the United States, where they have not learned to do this work yet. We are always trailing after them, and then finding out in the end that we have not attained any objective.

I am satisfied that this militia item for the Topographic Survey should be passed and that more money should be spent on it next year.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Transport and freight, $200,000.
Is there any money at the disposal of the Militia Department to look after the fag ends in connection with military matters that have to toe adjusted?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: If they strictly pertain to the war, there is. We have an allowance in the proposed demobilization vote. Almost every week some fag end turns up. Only to-day I think my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition brought one to my attention. There was another case on Monday brought to my attention by. my hon. friend from Stratheona (Mr. Douglas). Some men in Nova Scotia who wanted to get to the West, and should have gone to the West, had overstayed their time. A number of cases of that kind are continually cropping up, which we have to charge to demobilization.

I have a case in mind which might very well be called a fag end. It is the case of a man who was employed by the Military Service Branch at Halifax to go out into the country and trace up men who did not report. They gave him seven or eight warrants, and told him where to find the men. Some of them he found, and some of them he did not. Some, when they discovered that he was after them, went and reported themselves. The warrants were sent to this man with an absurd instruction to go and hunt for the men; if he found them, and was able to bring them to headquarters, he would get something, but if he did not find them and bring them to headquarters he would not get anything. He was an enthusiastic chap and started out on his search. He spent some weeks driving around the country with his own horse, paying his. own board, and spending a lot of time searching for these men. He sent in his return, and he was never paid one cent. It is a most extraordinary thing that this man should be put to the expense and trouble of going around the country searching for these men, and paying all his expenses, and then never get a cent at the end. His return was sent in to the department, and why he has never been settled with, I cannot understand.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I think I know the case to which my hon. friend has reference.
Strange as it may seem, I happened to be looking into it this morning. It is not a case which comes within the jurisdiction of the Militia Department. My hon. friend knows that the administration of the Military Service Act was under a committee in the Justice Department, and instructions were sent to this man in question from the Justice Department. He received the instructions from them and acted under their orders. My hon. friend has communicated with the Department of Militia on this subject, and in due course the papers came before me. I find that the instruc-tipns to the officer contained this clause, that if the man after whom he was sent proved on apprehension to be a defaulter, the constable or official would be paid his reasonable fees and expenses. If the man on apprehension prpved not to be a defaulter he would have received no allowance. Many of the men who were apprehended by this particular officer were r.ot defaulters, they were not liable under the Military Service Act. But the officer performed the service notwithstanding, and I think myself it is very unreasonable to deprive him of his reasonable fees and expenses. He performed the work'he was sent to perform by the Department of Justice, not by the Department of Militia. However, it is just a question from what fund the money should be paid. It does not relate to demobilization and my own opinion was we should ask for a Supplementary Estimate to pay the account. I was going to recommend it anyway, because I think it is a claim that ought to be paid.
I know this man very well. He is the deputy sheriff for the county of Victoria-

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: That is the man.
-and a very enthusiastic officer. He is not a young man by any means; he is about sixty years of age. He worked hard to find those men and it is extraordinary that he should not have been paid.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Warlike stores, $197,054.
I would like the minister to give an explanation of what these warlike stores are?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The pre-war vote for warlike stores was a very large one. In 1913-14 it was $703,375. Last year we asked for $400,000, and this year we are asking only $197,054 a reduction of $203,-

000. The whole purpose of the vote is for artillery stores, engineers' stores, medical stores, general stores, up-keep and any new services that may be established.
What are these stores?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Militia and Defence
stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Department of Public Works; Public buildings, New Brunswick, $86,500.
Of this item I notice that $83,500 is for the city of St. John, leaving only $3,000 for the remainder of the province. I would like the minister to give some explanation of this vote.

speakeroldname: Hon. F. B. McCURDY (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend will appreciate the position in which the department finds itself this year. As I explained to the committee on the occasion of the nocturnal sitting, the only items which are being voted this year are items of an unavoidable character. It happens that in the province of New Brunswick the buildings which demand attention this year are situated at large centres. Of the vote in question, $75,000 is required for one particular item in connection with the quarantine service. I am advised that the quarantine service requires these expenditures in the most urgent way. If the request had not been of the greatest urgency I would have hesitated to bring the Estimate before the committee.

This item of $75,000 for new buildings, repairs and improvements at the Partridge island quarantine station is a revote. As the money was not expended last year, I do not see any reason why it should be expended this year, and it would seem to me that the item is kept in the Estimates for a certain purpose-

so that at any time the money can be expended, if necessary, on certain interests. Therefore I would like to see it struck off this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
A part of this vote is already in the way of being expended. It will be no surprise to my hon. friend to know that the requests which have come in from the Immigration quarantine service are largely in excess of this vote, which is of a general character. The request that comes from the Department of Health for expenditures on quarantine service at St. John is under the following heads: Disinfector and power plant building- $ 76,000
New third class detention building. .	. .	100,000
Addition to existing third class building	 20,388
New wharf for low tide accommodation
two pairs semi-detached	houses..	..	30,000
New ice house	 1,200
Fencing	 1,400
Electric lighting system	 15,000
General alterations, repairs and furniture	 16,573
Is that all in connection with the quarantine station?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Yes, on Partridge
island, St. John. I can assure the Committee that if the vote of $75,000 towards this request for $260,000 is given the service will be able to take care of the immigration demands which will be made on the organization during the year.

The
fact that the people of St. John are asking for this expenditure is no reason why the committee should vote the money. Although they are modest about their requests for expenditure, they are always ready to take public money when they can get it. My hon. friend says that part of this $75,000 has already been spent. He must be mistaken, because according to the Estimates the whole of this sum is a revote. What is the explanation as to the necessity of this expenditure, and as to part of the money having already been spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

speechtext:
If we were in normal times I would not object to this vote, but I understand that the quarantine station on
Partridge island is in very fair condition, and as immigration is slackening I cannot understand why these large amounts are necessary at the present time, especially when applications for public buildings throughout the province of New Brunswick have been made to the department without result. Post office accommodation is needed in the city of Moncton, but there is no provision for it in the Estimates. Then again, many of our public buildings are in fogent need of repairs. Right in my own county there is a public building badly in need of external repairs, but I have not been successful in getting the department to attend to the matter. The building is in the middle of a two-acre plot and only the front of it has been painted; in fact, it is a case of washing the face and leaving the ears dirty. I am not asking for anything to be done this year because we must economize, but these are cases which certainly require attention just as much, if not more so, than the quarantine station at Partridge island. Therefore this $75,000 which was not expended last year certainly should not be expended this year.

In 1911 and before that application was made for a public building in my own town, which is a little larger than some of the small towns in the minister's province where the people have been given public buildings for several years past. During the last ten years the Treasury has received over half a million dollars in customs and post office revenues from my township, which is quite an item, and all the money has been spent throughout other parts of the country. Now I am informed that no public buildings will be erected this year, especially post offices. There is great necessity for a public building in the county of Madawaska, and I am urgently asked to interview the minister with a view to obtaining his favourable consideration to the erection of such a building. The population of my town is about six thousand. The post office is in a private building, and it is difficult for the public to be admitted when the mail arrives and is being sorted. When the minister is visiting some of the towns in his neighbouring province next summer I would like him to come to my town and see the conditions for himself. If he does, I am sure that he will realize how great is the necessity for the erection of a public building there, and for the provision of the required amount in the Estimates next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
If the hon. member
will refer to page 44 of the Estimates he will see that there is provided an item of $162,000 towards the building of an international bridge across the St. John river from Edmundston to the state of Maine. I am sure the hon. member will agree that it would scarcely be reasonable to ask for the erection of public buildings in his county in addition to a boon requiring that large expenditure.
Not this year; I mean next year.

My hon. friend has given as a reason for not acceding to the request of the member for Madawaska for a public building the fact that there is an item in the Estimates of $160,000 for the building of a bridge. I do not see anything in the Estimates to provide for the building of a bridge near my town, so the same objection could not be urged against the request which I have made for a post office and public building. However, that is not my reason for rising. We have heard a good deal of talk during the past two sessions about the League of Nations, but we hardly expected that one of the reasons given for the building of a quarantine station in St. John would be some demand or requirement on the part of the League of Nations. Now, I have had some correspondence and communications with the residents of St. John, and as far as I have been able to gather, that building is required there in order to meet the needs of the port, and I am glad that the minister is taking the necessary steps to have the work done. A great many immigrants go through Halifax and St. John, particularly during the winter months, and it is necessary that ample accommodation of this kind should be provided. The minister told us a few moments ago that part of this money had been expended. I commend the minister for having before him this evening the details with regard to certain matters in connection with which he was unable to inform us on a previous occasion. I would like to ask him now what part of this money has been expended, what work has been done so far, whether a contract has been let for any part of the work, and if so, what part.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
A portion of the vote
of which the item under consideration is a re-vote was required for the building of an addition to the third-class detention building at the St. John quarantine station, Partridge island. Tenders were called in December for the work, and four were

received, the lowest, that of Mr. J. E. Kane, $20,388.35, being accepted. The tenders ran from that figure up to $29,450. The lowest tender was accepted by authority of an Order in Council passed on January 10 of this year.

The minister mentioned
a sum of $260,000 requested by the Health Department for buildings at St. John, and he intimated that this vote of $75,000 was for the construction of buildings required for that department. Am I to understand that other buildings will be required later, involving the expenditure of additional money from year to year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The Department of Health advise that this work is most urgently needed; in fact they say they will not be answerable if the building is not provided this year. Accordingly the contract of which I have given particulars to the hon. member for Westmoreland has been awarded. The Department of Public Works is hopeful that the expenditure for this year will be confined to $75,000.

But will $75,000 be an
end of the expenditure on this account, or will it be necessary to make expenditures from time to time until $260,000 is spent?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The building is described to the Department of Public Works as a self-contained unit. We have no reason to anticipate that the construction of the building will involve any further expenditure.
I notice at the bottom of item 130 the words "Appropriations not required for 1921-22." What is the explanation of that item?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: It is rendered necessary by the system of accounting followed by the Department of Finance. It represents appropriations asked for last year, but not spent and not required for this year, and which simply lapse.

It is given here as
$18,500. The total vote, exclusive of the $75,000 re-voted, would not amount to $18,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The only way in which my hon. friend would be able to have that perfectly clear in his mind would be by referring to last year's Estimates. Certain sums which were voted a year ago were not all required; the money was not all spent, nor is a revote required this year to the extent of $18,500. That represents

the unexpended and unrequired balance of the vote authorized by Parliament a year ago.
The column at the extreme right of the page giving a comparison, 1920-21, gives the total, $103,000. Am I to understand that that total does not include revotes?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The item of $103,000 is the total vote passed a year ago. $18,500 of that vote has not been spent and is not required.
If the minister will look at the column, he will find that there is not $18,500 in the total. It would look as though there was a decrease in the expenditure for the item.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The total is $103,000, being made up of $2,500 for Moncton examining warehouse; $7,000 for St. John Dominion building, improvements; $75,000 for St. John quarantine station, and appropriations not sjient, $18,500.
The Estimates show only three main items for last year for purposes of comparison. Some item must have been left out. .

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The items making up $18,500 are left out because no appropriation in respect to any of those items are required this year.

I am somewhat puzzled as to the necessity of this item of $75,000. The hon. member for Kent (Mr. Leger)-and he is well versed in matters relating to New Brunswick- thinks that it is not necessary to make this expenditure this year. The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) thinks that it is required. The minister, when he is asked for an explanation, gives a dissertation from a memorandum supplied by the Deputy Minister of Health relating to the League of Nations, in which he tells us that in Central Europe there are certain diseases which require to be watched throughout the world, and amongst other places, the city of St. John. That is a very general statement. I should like to get a report from some man in charge of immigration in this country, showing that these further expenditures at St. John are necessary for immigration purposes; that this building is really needed for immigrants coming to St. John. Has the minister a report from the officer in charge instead of a far away story by the Deputy Minister of Health who
has given a general statement which covers not only the city of St. John, but every other part of the world, because it is necessary to prevent the spread of these diseases in St. John or anywhere else. We got along without this expenditure last year and the year before. Immigrants have been coming into St. John for many years. Is the number increasing? Why are we being asked for this large expenditure at this time when we want to save every dollar it is possible to save? The minister has not given a satisfactory explanation regarding this matter. I am not opposing it, but it is our duty in this committee to see that not one dollar is voted during the present session for any unnecessary purpose.

In the Estimates for New Brunswick there is an item- of $75,000 for quarantine purposes. If we look at the Estimates for Nova Scotia, we find that last year an amount of $250,000 was voted; that $100,000 was spent-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Nothing spent at all.

I would ask the minister to give an explanation with regard to that. For Nova Scotia there is an item of $250,000 voted last year and nothing spent. This year, $150,000 is asked for. There is an item of $200,000 for a quarantine station at Grosse Isle in Quebec, and those three items all read about the same. For the province of Nova Scotia the item reads:
Halifax quarantine station, new buildings.
For the province of New Brunswick the item reads:
St. John quarantine station, Partridge Island, new buildings, repairs and improvements.
For the province of Quebec the item reads:
Grosse Isle, quarantine station, new buildings and repairs.
Therefore, we must come to the conclusion that evidently the Government is having new buildings erected in those three places. If we take into consideration the fact that, during the years immediately previous to the war, immigration was about double what it is to-day. I wonder how it is that these new buildings are of such immediate importance that they should be built now, especially when we all agree that this is no time for erecting new buildings, although it is right enough to repair buildings when that is absolutely necessary. We all know that it costs to-day about 50 per cent more to erect new buildings than it will probably in five years

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: from now. Consequently, to erect new buildings at the present time is as bad an investment as can be made. The other day the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) said that for the last two years our immigration had been, on an average, 133,000 a year. For the three or four years previous to the war, the average immigration was over a quarter of a million. We are to-day asked for three appropriations in three provinces aggregating the enormous sum of $425,000. Why do we need additional buildings to-day at such an enormous cost to provide for an immigration which is only half what it was during years immediately previous to the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The answer is very
simple. The need for buildings of this character is not based on the total number of immigrants coming to the country, but rather on the necessity for guarding against contagious and infec-
10 p.m. tious diseases which come with these immigrants. I have read to the committee a memorandum prepared by the Department of Health and statements from other bodies, including the American Red Cross Society outlining present conditions in countries from which a certain portion of these immigrants come. As long as these scourges are raging in the countries of origin of these immigrants, I am sure members of the committee will agree that it is well for the authorities in this country to be on guard against such contingencies as the introduction of these communicable diseases into Canada. The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) was not present at the sitting last evening; otherwise, he would not have asked this question regarding the Halifax building. There are appropriations for necessary quarantine stations at St. John, Halifax and Quebec, the three large and important ports which are concerned with immigration. The responsibility for the efficiency, or, rather the efficacy of measures taken to provide against the introduction of diseases in connection with immigration, rests with the officials of the Health Department.
My hon. friend from Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) wanted a report from some of the immigration officials at Partridge island. The report which I read to the committee a few moments ago from the Deputy Minister of Health is more than that. It is based, so I am advised, on the reports of the immi-

gration officials at Partridge island, and also on the personal observations of the Deputy Minister of Health, who himself visited these places and passed upon the requirements. There may be a difference of opinion with regard to the total amount of the expenditures ' required. The Department of Health has asked for the sums that I have mentioned. No less than any member of this committee, those charged with the responsibility of erecting these buildings, would like to see the expenditures kept down to the lowest feasible amount. As I stated to the committee last evening, in the case of the Halifax station it would appear to be possible by the reconstruction of the quarantine station on Lawlor's island to give the necessary quarantine services called for, instead; of erecting new buildings elsewhere. However, I covered that question fully last evening. With regard to the St. John requisition, I am confident that this vote of $75,000, although it may not provide all the buildings which the Deputy Minister of Health thinks should be provided, will enable that department to carry on its service and at the same time avoid unnecessary expenditure of public money.

How
many patients can be accommodated at St John with the present facilities?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I have not that information here, but I shall be glad to get it and forward it to my hon. friend.
I think it is essential that we should have that information. I should also like to know how many patients were treated there during the year 1920.

The accommodation at
St. John used to be ample for the requirements. There are not so many immigrants coming in now, and I think the present accommodation should be sufficient.

I
think it is essential that the committee should be given the information that we hate asked for. We are asked to vote money for the erection of new buildings, but we have not been given a word of information as to whether or not the present facilities are sufficient to accommodate the immigrants that are coming there. That information is the first I would expect from the minister. Does the officer in charge at St. John say that he needs more room, that he has more patients than he can accommodate?

Every one of course, will agree with the general statement of the Deputy Minister of Health that the country ought to look after people who come in here with diseases, and I hope we have been doing that in the past; but we are now being asked to vote a sum of money for buildings in three provinces, and we have not been given a single item of information to show the necessity for this increased accommodation. The medical officer in 'charge of these patients at St. John must know something about it. If there is necessity for enlarging the present accommodation, why does he not say so? The statements made by the Deputy Minister of Health are very general. He did not come down to a single detail. He did not tell us for instance how many beds they had, how many wards they had, how many they would like, or how many patients they accommodated last year. He simply makes the general observation that under the League of Nations these matters must me looked after. With that statement, of course, everybody will agree, but the minister should give us detailed information on the points I have mentioned. As a business man I would expect him to look into this thing and satisfy himself that the expenditure is necessary. My hon. friend has a reputation in the Maritime Provinces as a hard-headed business man, and I would like him to maintain that reputation in the House of Commons. We have been looking forward to a successful administration'of the Department of Public Works under his management, and it would be very disappointing for us to think that he was going to embark upon an expenditure of this kind without having first satisfied himself that the expenditure is necessary. It may be necessary, but I do not thnk we have been given the details from the minister to show that it is absolutely necessary.

My hon. friend knows very well that it would hardly be possible for the Minister of Public Works to visit and personally inspect all these buildings to ascertain exactly what was required in the nature of additional accommodation. This vote which is now called in question, was assented to unanimously by the committee last year. I submit that I have sufficient- details to justify the committee in passing this item, but if there are any further details my hon. friend wishes to have, if he will express his wishes, I shall be very glad to secure the information from the Department of Health and forward it to him.

There is one line of argument that is followed by the minister which I think he should drop at the earliest possible moment. The mere fact that an item of expenditure may have slipped through the committee last year without any critical examination is no reason in the world why the same item should not be criticised when it comes up again this year. The fact that this committee made a mistake once and failed to do their duty ' is no reason why they should repeat the mistake.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I do not think they made a mistake last year.

It is our duty to get the facts. Last night we were kept here all hours of the night listening to the argument of the minister, that because the committee had passed a certain item last year they could not consistently oppose it this year. Man after man in the committee was put down by the minister with this argument: You voted for this last year; you have committed the unpardonable sin; you are not permitted to put forward an argument at all, because you were a mem-

ber of the committee that passed this item last year; it makes no difference whether you read the item or not, you were a member of the committee and the item went through; you are therefore held culpable. It is not for me to give any instructions to the minister. I think he can very well strike on a stronger argument and one that will give him very much less trouble than to say to members on this side that, because they happened to be hear last year when these items went through, therefore their mouths are shut and they are not allowed to say anything further in criticism. My hon. friend from Guysborough is always reasonable in connection with criticisms of this kind, and he says that he is not satisfied with the information given. It is not to be expected that the Minister of Public Works should go to any port and take dimensions of buildings and investigate the conditions, but he is supposed to have officers who will do this work. The necessity of protecting the interests of the country, as well as protecting the Department of Public Works, requires that an engineer of that department should visit the ground and report to the minister upon every item of expenditure of this class. If the minister says that he has a report from his engineer, after having visited, and examined these buildings in St. John, that the report is in favour of doing this work in order to meet the necessities of the port, and that the proper requirements in general have been complied with in connection with this vote, then there is no fault to find. The trouble is we have not that information. The minister does not appear to have it, or else he declines to impart it to the committee.
The minister mentioned a $75,000 re-vote. Was that not passed as a Supplementary Estimate last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I think it was a Supplementary Estimate last year.

If the minister takes the ground, as he did last night, that we must be regarded as supporting every item we do not vote against we shall in future have to vote against every item in order to save ourselves from the accusation of supporting everything that comes down to the House at all times. I think the minister is rather unfair to members of the Opposition in taking such a stand as that. Supplementary Estimataes are often hurriedly passed during the very last hours of the session. We are not responsible for

that, and yet the minister accuses us of supporting items because we did not vote against them. That is hardly a fair attitude for him to take.

I was in the House last year when these Estimates came up and I did not oppose them because I thought they were absolutely necessary. The votes were not expended, and up to last fall nothing was done. In October or November there was " a great demonstration " in St. John and tenders were invited immediately afterward. That is what causes me to entertain suspicions in connection with this expenditure.

I want to follow up my question and get an answer from the minister. Has he received any report from any of his officials in St. John, or in the province of New Brunswick, showing the necessity for this expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: The Deputy Minister of Health advises that his recommendation is based on the report of his officer at Patridge island, supplemented by its own personal observations.

If I
remember rightly the report that was read from the Deputy Minister of Health made no special reference to the necessity of having anything done at St. John-that is he gave no more details than are already in our possession?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I have read a long
statement of details, and I am perfectly willing to read the statement again if my hon. friend wishes me to do so.

I do
not think there is any necessity for that.
Who made the recommendation?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
The Deputy Minister
of Health.

If the report contains the answers to the questions I have asked I would like to have that information, but I did not gather that it does. One question was: What is the present accommodation for patients at that quarantine station? The other is: How many patients were treated last Jrear? These are the kind of details I want. A general statement as to the necessity of having facilities at these ports will be accepted by everybody, but what I am looking for is something special from the medical officer at St. John or some one in

authority, to show why an extension of the present equipment is required.
You already have a building for immigration purposes. Is this exepnditure to provide an addition to the old building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: This is for an extension to the existing accommodations. The information that the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough asks for is without doubt in the Department of Public Health. I have not that particular information in my notes but, as I have already told the committee, I will he glad to see that the hon. gentleman's request goes to the Department of Public Health and I am sure the information for which he asks will be forthcoming.
In the meantime what are we to do with the item?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

speechtext: I do not quite understand where the practice of dumping everything on the Department of Public Works originated. It is an old practice and one that apparently is hard to get away from. If the Militia Department wants an armoury I cannot understand why it should go to the Public Works Department, why it should not build that armoury itself, because the first-hand information is in that department. The same thing is true about the Department of Public Health. If that department needs quarantine buildings why does it not build them? It has in its possession first-hand information from its own officers and public money is at its disposal. Why then does it not undertake the construction of the necessary buildings under the supervision of its own officers? I am not blaming the minister for the practice that has grown up, but it would be a very wholesome custom for him when he is putting through items of expenditure that do not particularly belong to his own department to have here the deputy minister, or some other official, of the department concerned, with the necessary information. If that is not to be done we must insist upon getting the information from the minister himself and let him go into the highways and byways and get that information in the best way he can. It would be no great hardship to secure the attendance of the deputy minister of the department immediately interested. We must not be deprived of the necessary information because the items of expenditure do not relate particularly to the Department of Public Works. If the minister and his own officers, have not the information the item should stand until the officer is brought here who can give the committee in a business-like and straightforward way all the facts they require. Nobody wants to block the Estimates; nobody is refusing to provide needed accommodation at any Canadian port. It is only business for us, representing as we do the owners of the money invested, to see that everything is done in a right and proper way, that the necessary information is forthcoming, that there are no loop holes about it, and that no money will be expended ahead of time or to a greater extent than is necessary to meet the public interests.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In connection with this contract and other contracts of the department, is the practice followed of inserting fair wage schedules and conditions for the protection of labour?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Are those
schedules prepared by officers of the Department of Labour or of the Department of Public Works?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: By officers of the Department of Labour.

I would like to have the minister's attention for a few moments with regard to the item of $1,000 for accommodation for the Moncton examining warehouse. Last year the vote was $2,500. What building were the repairs made upon, and what is the building used for?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: This amount is required for the installation of a table and bunks for parcels in the Higgins building, 691 Main Street, Moncton, which is now occupied by the Customs Department as an examining warehouse.

The building which is now used as a post office and customs house in

Moncton was erected shortly after Confederation when the present city was a mere village. It was then located at What was supposed to be the centre of the community, but the city has grown in a direction away from that building, so that it is now located at the extreme end of the town and does not accommodate the public generally. Moncton being a railway centre has grown from year to year, but during the past eight or ten years it has made exceptionally rapid progress, until to-day it is a city of between twenty thousand and twenty-five thousand people. Under these circumstances it is unnecessary for me to take further time to convince the committee and the minister that the building in question is absolutely too small to accommodate the local business. Last year the net postal revenue from Moncton amounted to the large sum of $300,000. A few weeks ago I had occasion to be in Moncton and walking along one of the streets far removed from the business centre, in fact in one of the back streets, I found on the corner of a garage the sign of the customs house. My hon. friend must know that, if not a disgrace, such a condition of affairs is a very great inconvenience to the people, and undoubtedly they are entitled to better accommodation. What I am now saying I have already expressed to the minister personally, and I hope he will take action. Last week a delegation waited on him in regard to this matter, and I notice in the newspaper reports that they were received with very great courtesy by him. Having had a week to think it over, I sincerely trust that my hon. friend will now be able to tell me that he and his colleague from New Brunswick-* two young, active and influential members of Parliament-will be able to convince their colleagues that Moncton should be given fair and reasonable consideration in this regard.
What I have said as to Moncton applies with equal or possibly stronger force to the town of Sackville. Sackville is the seat of Mount Allison University, and hundreds of students, yea, this year up to a thousand, and we trust in a very few years from now thousands, will be attending the university from all over the Maritime Provinces as well as from other parts of the Dominion, spending three or four years there as citizens. Notwithstanding the requirements of these students as well as the regular residents of the town there is no acceptable place for any citizen to go and get his mail. The old fMr. Oopp.]
Kitchen Building which now does duty as a post office was ready to tumble down before I was born, and that is some time ago. As far back as 1911 or 1912 property was purchased for the erection of a new building, and it does seem to me that there is no good reason why my hon. friend should not make arrangements for the erection of this very necessary public building.
I know my hon. friend will say that I am inconsistent because while criticising the expenditure of money in other quarters I am at the same time asking for its expenditure in these particular localities. But there are many places in the province of New Brunswick where I would like to see public money expended in ordinary times, but where I would not ask any government to incur expenditure under present conditions. But I do say, as I said last night in regard to the Annapolis post office, that I believe the Government are under an implied contract with the people to supply them with reasonably proper facilities for the conduct of the public business. What is true of these two particular localities is true of other places, I have no doubt, and I would advise my hon. friend and the Government to go over their Estimates again and carefully cull out what can be dispensed with for the present in order that they may give to the people what is absolutely necessary for the proper conduct of their public business.
I sincerely trust that my hon. friend between now and the close of the session when the Supplementary Estimates are brought down will see his way clear, supported, as I say, by my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, who knows the situation better than I do, to have these two particular cases looked after. I want to take this opportunity of expressing as strongly as I can the importance of providing these two much needed public buildings.

included in the division of the Maritime Provinces?

separate estimate for every small enpendi-ture. These items run all the way from one dollar up, and they come out of this fund, which is administered by officials of the department, so far as my observation goes, with a great deal of care.
All I can say it that I hope the public buildings in Kent county will have their share?
